{{Short description|English mathematician and astrologer (1542–1632)}}
{{Use British English|date=August 2014}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2026}}
[[File:Thomas Allen.jpg|thumb|Thomas Allen, 18th-century engraving by [[James Bretherton]]]]
'''Thomas Allen (or Alleyn)''' (21 December 1542{{snd}}30 September 1632) was an English mathematician and [[astrologer]]. Highly reputed in his lifetime, he published little, but was an active private teacher of mathematics. He was also well connected in the English intellectual networks of the period.<ref name=ODNB>{{cite ODNB|id=387|title=Allen, Thomas|first=A. J.|last=Turner}}</ref>

==Early life==
He was born in [[Uttoxeter]], Staffordshire. He was admitted scholar of [[Trinity College, Oxford]], in 1561; and graduated as M.A. in 1567. In 1571 he left his college and fellowship, and moved to [[Gloucester Hall]].<ref name=ODNB/> He became known for his knowledge of antiquity, philosophy, and mathematics.<ref name="EB1911">{{EB1911|inline=y|wstitle=Allen, Thomas|volume=1|page=692}}</ref>

==At Gloucester Hall==
Gloucester Hall suited Allen, a sympathiser at least with [[Catholicism]], because there was no stringent religious observance required there; indeed there was no chapel in the Hall.<ref name=Digby>{{cite ODNB|id=7629|title=Digby, Kenelm|first=Michael|last=Foster}}</ref> Allen's beliefs have been classified as "church papist", but also his posture as "crypto-Catholic": a Catholic faith combined with outward conformity to the [[Church of England]].<ref>Foster, p. 99.</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Library |first=Bodleian |title=The Bodleian Library record|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XDooAQAAIAAJ|page=381|access-date=17 April 2012|year=1999|publisher=University Press.}}</ref> He joined there his friends Edmund Reynolds, Miles Windsor, and [[George Napper]], who had also left their colleges at a time of increasing religious tensions on Oxford; Napper was to be a Catholic martyr. Trinity shed six more of its Fellows within a few years.<ref>Foster, p. 104.</ref><ref>{{Cite CE1913|wstitle=Ven. George Napper}}</ref>

Allen encouraged other scholars to migrate there, such as [[John Budden]]<ref>{{cite ODNB|id=3882|title=Budden, John|first=Brian P.|last=Levack}}</ref> and [[William Burton (antiquary, died 1657)|William Burton]].<ref>{{cite ODNB|id=4142|title=Burton, William|first=Elizabethanne|last=Boran}}</ref> He had a wide range of pupils and followers: [[Kenelm Digby]]<ref name=Digby/> and [[Brian Twyne]]<ref>{{cite ODNB|id=27924|title=Twyne, Brian|first=A. J.|last=Hegarty}}</ref> in [[natural philosophy]], with [[Theodore Haak]] coming later.<ref>{{cite ODNB|id=11827|title=Haak, Theodore|first=A. G.|last=Keller}}</ref> The mathematical school of Allen included [[Thomas Harriot]] and [[Walter Warner]],<ref>{{cite ODNB|id=14045|title=Hues, Robert|first=Susan M.|last=Maxwell}}</ref> and [[John Davies (poet, born 1569)|Sir John Davies]] (to whom Allen taught Catholic doctrine).<ref>{{cite ODNB|id=7242|title=Davies, Sir John|first=J. J. N.|last=McGurk}}</ref>

Mathematical geography was an important topical subject in which Allen was reputed, pursued by several groups in England, including another around [[Henry Briggs (mathematician)|Henry Briggs]]: Allen may have taught the geographer [[Richard Hakluyt]]. He did teach [[Robert Fludd]] and [[Sir Thomas Aylesbury]].<ref name="Cormack1997">{{cite book |last=Cormack |first=Lesley B.|author-link= Lesley Cormack |title=Charting an Empire: Geography at the English Universities, 1580–1620|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kq0iwPQm92AC&pg=PA124|access-date=17 April 2012|date=22 December 1997|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-11606-8|page=124}}</ref> In the humanities there were [[Robert Hegge]],<ref>{{cite ODNB|id=12865|title=Hegge, Robert|first=Vivienne|last=Larminie}}</ref> and [[William Fulbecke]].<ref>{{cite ODNB|id=10221|title=Fulbecke, William|first=D. R.|last=Woolf}}</ref> When the [[Camden Chair of Ancient History]] was being set up in the early 1620s, Allen successfully supported the candidacy of [[Degory Wheare]] with [[William Camden]]; and a few years later, in 1626, Wheare came to Gloucester Hall as Principal.<ref>{{cite ODNB|id=29180|title=Wheare, Diagory|first=J. H. M.|last=Salmon}}</ref>

Allen died at Gloucester Hall.

==Other associations==
Allen corresponded with [[Henry Percy, 9th Earl of Northumberland]].<ref name="Cormack1997"/> Northumberland invited Allen to visit, and he spent some time with the [[Syon House]] group around the Earl; he became acquainted with [[Thomas Harriot]], [[John Dee (mathematician)|John Dee]], and other mathematicians. He also knew well [[Robert Bruce Cotton|Sir Robert Cotton]], [[William Camden]], and their antiquarian associates.<ref name="EB1911"/> He pointed out the historian [[Æthelweard (historian)|Æthelweard]] (Fabius Quaestor) to Camden.<ref>[http://www.philological.bham.ac.uk/cambrit/angsaxeng.html philological.bham.ac.uk, ''Camden'', English-Saxons.]</ref>

==Astrologer==
Allen was noted as astrologer to [[Robert Dudley, 1st Earl of Leicester]], as Dee was for [[Elizabeth I of England|Queen Elizabeth]].<ref>[[A. L. Rowse]], ''Simon Forman: Sex and Society in Shakespeare's Age'' (1974), p. 7.</ref> Foster believes Allen probably met Leicester through Lady Paulet, wife of [[Hugh Paulet]], née Elizabeth Blount, who was the widow of [[Sir Thomas Pope]], the founder of Trinity College, Oxford.<ref>Foster, p. 120.</ref>

There is a surviving 62-page [[horoscope]] cast for the teenage [[Philip Sidney]] in the Ashmole manuscripts in the [[Bodleian Library]], in the period 1570–2 when he was studying at Oxford, where Leicester was Chancellor, and it has been attributed to Allen; the case has also been made that it was by Dee. A link between the two is that [[Edward Kelley]] is said to have worked briefly for Allen.<ref>Katherine Duncan-Jones, ''Sir Philip Sidney, Courtier Poet'' (1991), pp. 50–1.</ref><ref>Peter J. French, ''John Dee: The World of an Elizabethan Magus'', p. 129 note 4, and p. 113 note 2.</ref> Allen definitely cast a natal horoscope for [[Robert Pierrepont, 1st Earl of Kingston-upon-Hull|Robert Pierrepont]] (1584), and cast also for [[William Herbert, 3rd Earl of Pembroke]], a later Chancellor of Oxford, in 1626.<ref>Foster, p. 124.</ref>

==Reputation==
Allen's skill in mathematics and astrology earned him the credit of being a [[Magician (paranormal)|magician]]. In an incident related in [[John Aubrey]]'s ''[[Brief Lives]]'', it was in a visit to [[Holme Lacy]] as the guest of [[John Scudamore (courtier)|Sir John Scudamore]] that the servants threw his ticking watch into the [[moat]], thinking it the Devil.<ref>[[Hugh Trevor-Roper]], ''Archbishop Laud'' (2000), p. 62.</ref> The author of ''[[Leicester's Commonwealth]]'' accuses him of employing the art of "figuring" to further the earl of Leicester's unlawful designs, and of endeavouring by the "black art" to bring about a match between his patron and the Queen.<ref name="EB1911"/> There Allen's name is coupled with Dee's as [[atheist]]s, in a series of claims that Leicester found physicians and other lackeys for his evil-doing at Oxford and elsewhere.<ref>[[Frank J. Burgoyne]], ''History of Queen Elizabeth, Amy Robsart and the Earl of Leicester being a reprint of "Leycesters commonwealth", 1641'' (1904), pp. 99–100; [https://archive.org/stream/historyofqueenel04leycuoft#page/98/mode/2up archive.org].</ref>

After his death, funeral orations praising Allen were given by [[William Burton (antiquary, died 1657)|William Burton]] and George Bathurst (1610–1644).<ref name=DNB>{{cite DNB|wstitle=Allen, Thomas (1542-1632)|display=Allen, Thomas (1542–1632)}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Society |first=Royal |author-link=Royal Society |title=Notes and records of the Royal Society|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jLkvAAAAIAAJ|page=194|access-date=16 April 2012|year=1973|publisher=Royal Society of London}}</ref> Burton's retailed the story of how Leicester had offered a bishopric to Allen, who declined the offer. Allen in fact was, by choice, not in holy orders.<ref>Forster, p. 127.</ref>

==Works==
He wrote a Latin commentary on the second and third books of [[Claudius Ptolemy]] of [[Pelusium]], ''Concerning the Judgment of the Stars'', or, as it is commonly called, ''Of the Quadripartite Construction, with an Exposition''. He also wrote notes on [[John Bale]]'s ''De Scriptoribus M. Britanniae''.<ref name="EB1911"/>

==Library and legacy==
Allen collected manuscripts relating to history, [[ancient history|antiquity]], [[astronomy]] and [[astrology]], philosophy, and mathematics. At least 250 items from his library can still be traced.<ref name=ODNB/> He also acquired manuscripts from dissolved monasteries, such as [[Reading Abbey]], for which his sources may have been [[Gerbrand Harkes]], the Protestant dealer, and Clement Burdett.<ref>{{cite book |last=Coates |first=Alan |title=English Medieval Books: The Reading Abbey Collections from Foundation to Dispersal|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gZVtP5dONY8C&pg=PA138|access-date=17 April 2012|date=22 April 1999|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-820756-6|page=138}}</ref> While in Allen's possession, most of his manuscripts were unbound or had simple covers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Thomas ALLEN 1540?-1632 |url=https://www.bookowners.online/Thomas_Allen_1540%3F-1632 |access-date=29 September 2022 |website=Book Owners Online}}</ref>

A considerable part of Allen's collection was presented to the [[Bodleian Library]] by Sir Kenelm Digby, to whom it had been left:<ref name="EB1911"/> over 200 manuscripts, which were rebound in calf. This bequest was strong in works by early English scientists, including [[Roger Bacon]], [[Simon Bredon]], [[John Eschenden]], [[Robert Grosseteste]], John Sharp, and [[Richard Wallingford]]. But Allen's library was in flux during his lifetime, as he lent or gave items, and was consulted by others. He was a significant supporter of [[Sir Thomas Bodley]]'s effort to found the Library; and gave it a number of works. Some went to the [[Cottonian Library]], presumably via [[Richard James (scholar)|Richard James]]. Sir Thomas Aylesbury, another former pupil,<ref name="Cormack1997"/> was another one of Allen's major legatees.<ref name="Horner2007">{{cite book |last=Horner |first=Patrick J. |title=The Index of Middle English Prose: Handlist III: A Handlist of Manuscripts Containing Middle English Prose in the Digby Collection, Bodleian Library|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KQY6hAApi3oC&pg=PR10|access-date=17 April 2012|date=16 August 2007|publisher=Boydell & Brewer Ltd|isbn=978-1-84384-151-7|pages=x–xi}}</ref> The [[Cuthbert Gospel of St John]], seen in his library by [[James Ussher]], appears to have left his possession by 1622, as it is not in a catalogue of that date. Ussher wrote to Camden in 1606 of the help he had had from Allen's collection, consulting [[William of Malmesbury]], and a papal bull from [[Giraldus Cambrensis]] via Johannes Rossus.<ref>[[Charles Richard Elrington]] ''The Whole Works of the Most. Rev. James Ussher D.D.'' vol. 15 (1864), pp. 5–18; [https://archive.org/stream/cu31924024758959#page/n21/mode/2up archive.org].</ref>
